title: LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B
gist: IBM Granite releases experimental 3B and 8B Granite 4.1 preview models trained on LLMON, a markup language whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens, explicitly separating instructions from data. IBM claims this nearly eliminates static indirect prompt injection on the OPI benchmark (47% more attacks avoided than the best frontier model tested) while holding general capability on par with Granite 4.1 Instruct.

themes.theme: Context structure as the root of LLM brittleness

insights.claim: IBM's Granite team argues that LLM contexts carry rich structure (system prompts, past turns, tool responses, requirements, reasoning chains) that is either implicit or encoded in formats like JSON not designed for LLMs, which is a main reason small LLMs are brittle and vulnerable to prompt injection.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Positions input-format design, not just model scale, as a lever for reliability and security of small enterprise models.
insights.quote: This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways.
insights.locator: LLMs rely on their context to generate

insights.claim: JSON is poorly suited to causal language models because its structural tokens ({, ", :) also appear in normal text, escaping rules are only statistical patterns to a model, and nesting depth relies on bracket counting, which transformers are weak at over long spans.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Challenges the industry default of JSON-structured prompting and structured outputs, implying a market for LLM-native formats and tooling.
insights.quote: JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models.

insights.claim: LLMON (LLM Object Notation) is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content occupy separate parts of the vocabulary, and nesting is stated locally so the model need not track hierarchy over long spans.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: A tokenizer-level design choice that competitors could replicate; signals structure-aware training as an emerging differentiation axis.
insights.locator: LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup

insights.claim: LLMON uses unique block IDs to bind instructions anywhere in the context to the data payloads they act on, analogous to calling functions with arguments in programming languages; IDs are drawn from a fixed set encoded as single tokens, so addressing any block costs two tokens.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Low token overhead suggests the approach can scale to long agentic contexts without meaningful cost penalty.
insights.locator: The two-character block IDs are drawn

insights.claim: On the OPI benchmark, which places injections in the data of classic NLP tasks, all tested non-LLMON open- and closed-source models carried out injected instructions with high probability, while the LLMON previews practically eliminated the problem.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: If it holds up, instruction/data separation is a concrete security feature for enterprise agent and RAG deployments where injection is a top adoption blocker.
insights.quote: All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability.

insights.claim: IBM reports the LLMON preview models avoid 47% more prompt-injection attacks than the best frontier model it tested and 95% more than the best open-source model, with similar trends on the ASB and StruQ benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: A small open model claiming a large security edge over frontier models could shift procurement criteria toward security-by-architecture.
insights.quote: avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model
insights.locator: All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible

insights.claim: The benchmarks used test only static indirect prompt injections; IBM says it is still working on adaptive attacks that unfold over many chat turns, and stresses the privilege rule is a learned behavior rather than an enforced guarantee.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Limits the security claim: multi-turn adaptive attacks remain unsolved, so this is not yet a production-grade defense.
insights.quote: This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee.
insights.locator: The resulting privilege rule falls out

insights.claim: Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models, so IBM claims the injection-robustness gains come without loss of general capability.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Removes the usual safety-vs-capability tradeoff objection, easing a drop-in swap for existing Granite users.
insights.quote: Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability.

insights.claim: The LLMON models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than instruct models, and a conventional instruction-tuning corpus (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling) was re-serialized into LLMON with each turn carrying an execution block naming the instruction, inputs, and output location.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Shows the approach is a post-training data reformatting rather than new pretraining, making it cheap for other labs to copy.

insights.claim: Training data is augmented with decoy instruction and data blocks deliberately left unbound while the target output is unchanged, teaching the model to follow only dependencies dictated by the execution block.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: The decoy-augmentation mechanism is the core of the injection resistance and is a transferable technique.
insights.locator: In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions

insights.claim: After supervised tuning, the models went through five sequential GRPO reinforcement-learning stages (multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, math) and a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model's own responses to injection attempts.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Illustrates that relatively small targeted preference datasets (about a thousand pairs) can harden models against specific attack classes.

insights.claim: Under LLMON, an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is treated as material to read, and unreferenced spans are ignored.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: A privilege hierarchy for context content is exactly what agentic tool-use security needs; watch for similar schemes from other model vendors.
insights.quote: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow.
insights.locator: The resulting privilege rule falls out

insights.claim: IBM released two experimental preview models, granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview, plus a GitHub toolkit, and labels them ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Commercial impact is deferred; this is a research preview to seed developer mindshare for Granite.
insights.quote: This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

insights.claim: LLMON enriches rather than replaces chat templates: developers keep calling apply_chat_template with a messages list, but can name parts of a turn (instruction, data, requirement) and mark each exec True or False, and the shipped template renders the LLMON blocks.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Low integration friction lowers switching costs for teams already on Granite 4.1 3B or 8B.
insights.locator: How is LLMON related to chat templates?

insights.claim: IBM provides lossless JSON-to-LLMON converters and native LLMON support in its Mellea framework, which automatically LLMONizes LLM calls, targeting teams with existing JSON pipelines.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Tooling around the format is IBM's lever to build an ecosystem around Granite and its generative-computing stack.
insights.locator: Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON

insights.claim: LLMON supports custom domain vocabularies via LoRA adapters; IBM demonstrated this on the ScienceWorld benchmark with tags such as instr.task.goal and data.state.inventory, training an adapter on reference solutions that then played held-out games.
insights.speaker: Abraham Daniels
insights.so_what: Suggests a path for structured agent workflows in enterprise domains using small fine-tuned models.
